c1.story:
Insurance is the strangest business on the market. A factory knows its costs before it sets a price. An insurer sets the price first and finds out its costs years later, when the claims come in. A life insurer may not know whether a policy was profitable until the policyholder turns eighty.

That one oddity splits the industry into doors that behave nothing alike. Life insurers, LIC, SBI Life, HDFC Life, ICICI Prudential Life, sell protection against dying too early and savings plans that run for ten, twenty or thirty years. Their profit is a promise: it trickles in over the life of each policy, so the market values them on how much future profit each year's sales lock in, a number called value of new business, rather than on this year's reported earnings.

General insurers, ICICI Lombard, Go Digit, New India Assurance, sell one-year covers for cars, factories, crops and company health plans. Their profit shows up every quarter as the gap between premiums and claims, plus the interest earned on premiums before claims are paid. Standalone health insurers, Star Health and Niva Bupa, are a specialised version selling only retail health, where the claims are hospital bills and the enemy is medical inflation. And at the back sits the reinsurer, GIC Re, which insures the insurers: it takes a share of their big risks, the factory fire, the cyclone, the flood, for a share of their premium.

A life insurer sells a promise and books it over decades. A general insurer sells a year and finds out by Diwali whether it priced it right.

All four tiles carry the same medium or low profit bar, and that is worth pausing on. Insurance is not a business where anyone keeps a fat, easy margin. The regulator caps expenses, the banks that sell the policies take their cut, and claims are, by design, most of the premium. The winners are the ones that do the ordinary things slightly better for a very long time.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each from top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it tell you what is sold and how profit arrives: slowly over a policy's life for life insurers, quarterly as underwriting plus float income for general insurers, as hospital bills against premiums for health insurers, and as a share of other insurers' risks for the reinsurer.
  • The tickers are listed names behind each door. Click one for its stock page. LICI sits with the private life names even though it is state-owned; it is still the largest life insurer by policies.
  • The profit bar is medium for the first three doors and low for the reinsurer. Life insurers keep a fair share because retail buyers rarely shop on price, but banks and the regulator take their cut. General and health insurers keep a fair share when they price with discipline. The reinsurer keeps the least: it takes the lumpiest risks, faces global competitors on price and has the least control over what it insures.
  • The bet line names the one variable each door depends on: new-business profit for life, underwriting discipline for general, out-running hospital inflation for health, and a quiet catastrophe year for the reinsurer.

The so-what line under the analogy is the most practical sentence here. A life insurer's profit is a value number published with results; a general or health insurer's is the quarterly gap between premium and claims. So the same quarter can look great for one door and poor for another for reasons that have nothing to do with management. Before comparing two insurers, check they sit behind the same door.

c2.story:
Follow a policy from idea to claim and you pass through five stations. The interesting part is that the insurer stands at only some of them, and the most powerful station is one it often does not own.

The first station is product and pricing. Actuaries, the mathematicians of the trade, design the cover and price it from mortality tables, claims history and interest rates. Since 2022 the regulator has let insurers launch most products without prior approval, a regime called use and file, which made this station faster.

The second station is distribution, and this is where the power sits. Most private life insurance and much general insurance in India is sold across a bank counter, very often by a bank in the same group: SBI sells SBI Life, HDFC Bank sells HDFC Life, ICICI Bank sells ICICI Prudential Life and ICICI Lombard, Axis Bank sells Axis Max Life. LIC has its famous army of agents. Online aggregators and point-of-sale agents fill the gaps. Every one of them takes a commission, and the bank's choice of whose policy to push can make or break an insurer's year.

The third station is underwriting and capital: accepting the risk and holding enough capital behind it to stay above the regulator's solvency floor. The fourth is reinsurance. Big or lumpy risks are passed on in part, by law first to GIC Re, which receives a slice of every general policy, then to foreign reinsurers such as Swiss Re and Munich Re through their Indian branches.

The last station is where the money finally moves: premiums invested in government bonds and shares until claims fall due, and claims settled through hospitals, garages, surveyors and third-party administrators. A health insurer's fate is decided here, in thousands of hospital billing counters it does not control.

In Indian insurance, whoever owns the bank counter owns the growth. Everything else is execution.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right: a policy is designed, sold, underwritten, partly reinsured, and finally paid out.

  • Each box names the station, what happens there and who stands there. Look at the second box: it names the parent banks, LIC's agents and online aggregators, not the insurers. That is the distribution point from the story.
  • The first band row shows who holds each station. Stations one and three are in the Indian colour: product design and underwriting are the insurers' own work. Station two, banks and agents, is uncoloured, because the seller is a different company, even when it shares a group name. Station four is in the rival colour: GIC Re stands there by law, alongside foreign reinsurers. Station five, hospitals and garages, is uncoloured too.
  • The second band row shows where the rival stands: foreign reinsurers and insurers, now allowed to own an Indian insurer outright. The rival label stretches across the first four stations. That is the change the new law brings: a foreign group can now design, sell, underwrite and reinsure in India on its own account, rather than as a junior partner. Only the last cell, the local hospital and garage network, is left to the wider world.

Then read the note: banks own the customer, LIC still leads individual life by policies, and the state general insurers lose share every year. The so-what turns that into a rule for the stock. A bank parent pushing a rival product, or a regulator capping what the bank can earn, moves an insurer more than any ad campaign. When you study an insurer, study its distribution mix first.

c3.story:
Who buys insurance in India, and why? The honest answer, for much of the industry's history, was that people bought it to save tax, or because a bank manager suggested it with a loan, and only occasionally because they actually wanted protection. That is changing, slowly, and the change is the investment case.

Start with salaried families. They buy term cover, savings plans and retail health. For decades the push came from the tax deduction for insurance premiums. The new income tax regime, made the default in 2023, offers no such deduction, so the tax reason is fading. What replaced it, at least briefly, was fear: Covid in 2020 and 2021 made millions of families realise what a hospital bill or an early death could do to them, and term and health sales jumped.

Bank customers buy policies bundled with accounts and loans. When you take a home loan and the bank suggests a cover to protect it, you are this tile. It is volume that rises and falls with bank credit growth and branch sales targets, and the regulator watches it closely for mis-selling.

Employers buy group health and group term cover for staff. This is enormous volume and thin margin, because companies shop their renewals every year and state insurers have historically priced for share. Vehicle owners buy motor cover, of which the third-party part is compulsory by law and priced by the government. Businesses buy fire, property, marine and engineering cover, priced off global reinsurance rates. Farmers buy crop insurance through the national scheme, with governments paying much of the premium, sometimes late. And retirees buy annuities that pay a monthly income for life.

Notice how different the motives are. Some buy out of fear, some because the law says so, some because the bank asked, some because their employer did it for them.

Retail is where the margin is and group is where the volume is. Growth built on the second is worth less than it looks.
c3.read:
Each tile is a customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who buys.
  • The second line is what they buy: term, savings, health, bundled covers, group plans, motor, property, crop, annuities.
  • The third line is what moves them, your watch list outside insurance: income growth and tax rules, bank sales targets and loan growth, hiring and medical inflation, vehicle sales and the third-party price, the capex cycle and global reinsurance prices, the monsoon and state payments, and bond yields for annuities.

A helpful way to read the grid is to sort the tiles by who decides. In salaried families and retirees, the buyer decides, and these are the high-margin tiles. In bank customers, the bank decides. In employers and businesses, a procurement team decides, on price. In vehicle owners and farmers, the law or the government decides.

Then match the tiles to the doors. Life insurers draw on salaried families, bank customers and retirees, and the margin depends on how much is pure protection versus savings. General insurers draw on employers, vehicle owners, businesses and farmers. Standalone health insurers live in the retail part of the first tile, which is why they carry the most medical-inflation risk.

The so-what line gives the warning: a quarter of fast growth built on group or credit-linked business is worth less than it looks. When an insurer reports strong premium growth, check which tile it came from. Retail protection growth is the real thing; a burst of group renewals at keen prices is volume borrowed at the cost of margin.

c4.story:
An insurer's accounts look upside down to anyone used to reading a manufacturer's. The customer pays first. The insurer delivers, by paying a claim, later, sometimes decades later. In between, it holds the customer's money and invests it. That pile of money is called the float, and it changes everything about how profit works.

Start with general and health insurance, where the picture is clearest. Premiums come in; claims and expenses go out. Add the two as a share of premium and you get the combined ratio. Below a hundred per cent, the insurer made money on underwriting itself. Above it, the insurer paid out more than it took in. Here is the surprise: many general insurers run combined ratios slightly above a hundred and still make a decent profit, because the float earns bond interest in the months between premium and claim. Losing a little on every policy and making it up on the float is a legitimate business model, as long as rates stay high enough and the losses stay small.

In health, the claims ratio has a built-in creep. Hospital tariffs rise faster than consumer prices year after year, so a health insurer that does not reprice every year sees its margin erode automatically. In motor, the third-party piece is priced by the government, while court awards for accident victims keep rising.

Life insurance is a different animal again. Reported profit is a poor guide, because the cost of acquiring a policy, the commission and the setup, lands in the first year, while profit trickles in for decades. So life insurers publish value of new business, the present value of future profits from this year's sales, and embedded value, the present value of the whole book plus net worth.

The line that ties them all together is solvency: the capital held above the regulator's floor. Fast growth eats capital, and an insurer close to the floor must either slow down or sell shares.

An insurer is paid to wait. The skill is in pricing the risk; the profit is often in what the money earns while waiting.
c4.read:
The two charts walk a hundred rupees of premium down to profit for life and general insurers. Read bar by bar, and notice what the charts leave out.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees of premium.
  • The input bar is claims, benefits and reserves set aside. It takes roughly three quarters of premium for life insurers, which includes money reserved for future maturities and deaths, and about seven of every ten rupees for general insurers.
  • The opex bar is commissions, people and branches. It takes a little under a fifth for life, and more than a quarter for general, where every one-year policy must be sold again next year.
  • The third bite, depreciation and interest, is a sliver in both charts. Insurers own no plant and carry little debt.
  • The last bar is what is left from underwriting. Life keeps a modest slice. General keeps almost nothing: that thin bar is the combined ratio sitting just under a hundred.

Now the key point. These walks show premium only. They do not show investment income on the float, which is where a general insurer actually makes most of its profit, and they cannot show a life insurer's future profits, which is what value of new business measures. That is why the so-what says: read value of new business for life, the combined ratio for general and health, because reported profit hides both. These are illustrative shapes; hover a bar for the amount.

The lines below mark claims, commissions, float income and solvency as yeses, and depreciation, capex, working capital and interest as noes. Working capital is a no for a happy reason: customers pay first.

c5.story:
Insurance is not cyclical the way steel or cement is. People do not stop dying or getting sick in a recession. Demand grows with incomes, quietly, year after year. So why did listed insurers soar after 2020 and then spend two years de-rating? Because in this industry the cycle is written in rulebooks and budget speeches, not in commodity prices.

The boom began with Covid. For the first time, millions of Indian families saw, close up, what an early death or a hospital stay could cost. Term and health sales jumped. Then the second wave in the first quarter of FY22 brought a flood of death and hospital claims, and global reinsurers raised the rates they charged Indian life insurers for term cover. Still, the market loved the penetration story, and listed insurers traded at rich multiples of embedded value.

The peak arrived in 2022 and early 2023. LIC listed in May 2022 in what was then India's biggest share sale, and promptly traded below its issue price. Private life margins hit records. Then the February 2023 budget announced that maturity proceeds from traditional policies with annual premiums above five lakh rupees would be taxed from April. Buyers rushed to beat the deadline, and Q4 FY23 sales spiked. After it, high-ticket savings sales slumped.

The bust was a series of rule changes landing one after another. New expense limits replaced commission caps from April 2023. From October 2024, surrender values rose, so customers who quit early got more of their money back, cutting margins on savings plans. Each change was defensible; together they reset the economics.

The bottom came in 2025: commissions renegotiated, margins reset lower but steady, and in September GST on individual life and health premiums was removed, cheaper for buyers, though insurers lost their input tax credit. Now retail protection and health volumes are responding.

In insurance, the bust did not come from customers walking away. It came from the regulator rewriting the menu.
c5.read:
Three parts: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years are the last cycle: the Covid boom of 2020 to 2022, the LIC-listing and pre-tax-change peak of 2022 and 2023, the rule-change bust of 2023 and 2024, and the 2025 bottom. The arrow sits just short of the top, at the very end of the bottom arc and about to cross into boom: early up-cycle. Hover an arc to read its story. Keep the explainer's own verdict in mind: this cycle is mild, and it is driven by rules more than by demand.

The timeline runs from 2019. A neutral 2019, a boom-coloured Covid stretch, a neutral 2022 for the LIC listing and the reform push, a bust-coloured 2023 and 2024 for the tax, expense and surrender changes, a neutral 2025 for GST removal and full foreign ownership, and 2026 marked now.

The four hands:

  • Value of new business margin: reset lower and stabilising, a mixed arrow. Rising would mean the mix is shifting to protection; falling would mean a rule is biting again.
  • Retail protection and health sales: strong after the GST cut, arrow up. The question is whether this is real penetration or a one-off price effect.
  • Health and motor combined ratio: slightly above breakeven, red arrow down. This is the weak hand. Above a hundred means claims and costs exceed premium.
  • Bond yields: drifting lower, mixed. Good for bond portfolios today, but lower yields cut the margin on guaranteed plans tomorrow.

The so-what below tells you who benefits first: insurers with a retail and protection mix. Names that grew on bank-led savings plans must first show margins have stopped falling.

c6.story:
Two dials with three dots each sit at the top of this table, and they could not be more different. One is a regulator's circular. The other is the stock market.

The first is the insurance regulator's rulebook. IRDAI sets how much an insurer may spend on commissions and expenses, how much a customer gets back on surrender, which products may be launched and how much capital must be held. Since 2023 almost every margin reset in this industry began with an IRDAI circular. The direction is one-way for the shareholder: tighter rules cut margins, usually starting the following quarter.

The second is equity markets. When the Nifty is rising, savers buy unit-linked plans, policies whose value tracks a market fund, and life insurers' embedded value rises with the shares they hold. A good market year flatters life insurers twice: more sales, and a richer book.

Then come the two-dot dials. Government bond yields are two-faced. Higher yields mean more income on the float and make annuities more attractive, but they also mark down existing bond holdings in the short term. Medical inflation pushes health claims up, because hospital bills rise faster than general prices. Income tax rules decide whether savings policies still carry a tax reason to buy; every break removed means fewer sold. Natural catastrophes, floods in Chennai in 2015 and Kerala in 2018, cyclones on the east coast, hit property and crop claims for general insurers and the reinsurer.

The one-dot dials are smaller but real. Short-term rates and fixed-deposit rates make savings plans look worse when they rise. Vehicle sales bring new motor policies. Bank credit growth brings credit-linked covers sold alongside loans.

What is missing is almost as telling. There is no commodity, no currency, no China. Insurance is one of the most domestic businesses on the market.
c6.read:
Each row is a dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches insurer profits: through rules, sales, investment income or claims.
  • A rise does: a green up arrow means a rise helps, a red down arrow means it hurts, and a diamond means it cuts both ways. Equity markets, vehicle sales and bank credit are green. The regulator's rules, short-term rates, medical inflation, tax rules and catastrophes are red. Bond yields are the diamond.
  • Weight: one to three dots. The two three-dot rows are the regulator and the stock market.

The last column shows today's reading where we track a series: the Nifty, a government bond fund for yields, the money market rate, the health component of consumer prices, the auto index and the bank index. The regulator, tax rules and catastrophes show a dash, because no price series captures them; for those, the news is the series.

Notice that most of the green rows are about sales and most of the red rows are about margins. That is the industry's tension in one table: volume depends on markets and banks, margin depends on regulators and hospitals.

Use it door by door. For a life insurer, read the regulator, the Nifty, bond yields and tax rows. For a health insurer, read medical inflation above all. For a general insurer and the reinsurer, read catastrophes and vehicle sales. The so-what gives the short version: watch the regulator's circulars and the equity market; one sets the margin, the other sets the mood of the savings buyer.

c7.story:
India is famously under-insured. Insurance premiums as a share of the economy are well below the global average, and for twenty years every insurer's investor presentation has opened with that gap. So why has the gap closed so slowly? The bottlenecks answer that, and they explain why insurance stocks have rewarded patience less than the penetration story promised.

The first is that the banks hold the customer. Most private life insurers sell the bulk of their policies through one or two banks, often a group parent. That is a superb channel while it lasts. But a bank answers to its own shareholders. When the regulator allowed banks to tie up with many more insurers in 2022, a bank could suddenly sell several insurers' policies from the same counter. An insurer that loses its place at the counter can see growth halve overnight.

The second is that the rules keep changing the economics. Tax, expenses, surrender values and GST have each reset margins since 2023, and two more are already announced: risk-based capital and a new insurance accounting standard. The third is trust. Savings plans sold as investments, claims rejected on technicalities, policies lapsing after a year: all of these keep buyers wary and the regulator watchful.

For health insurers, the defining bottleneck is hospital bills. Hospital tariffs rise faster than consumer prices, and India has no national price standard for procedures, so every year the same surgery costs more. A health insurer must reprice every year just to stand still.

India's insurance gap is real. So is the reason it closes slowly: the customer trusts the bank more than the policy.

Then come the smaller bottlenecks: a government-set motor third-party price that rarely keeps up with court awards, the constant need for fresh capital at fast growers, state general insurers underpricing to keep share, and floods and cyclones that strike the same coastal cities again and again.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites and a severity label. Use the label to decide where each risk belongs.

  • Structural: bank partners holding the customer, low trust and mis-selling, and hospital bill inflation. Three permanent features, and they cap the returns of the whole industry. They belong in your valuation.
  • Recurring: rules changing the economics, and public-sector pricing. The first is the one that has moved these stocks most since 2023; the second is why group health and fire rates stay thin.
  • Slow: the regulated motor third-party price, an old grievance that moves at the pace of government.
  • Cyclical: capital hunger. Smaller insurers need fresh capital in growth phases, which dilutes shareholders.
  • Two-sided: catastrophe concentration. Floods and cyclones hit property books hard, but a bad catastrophe year is also what lets general insurers and reinsurers push prices up afterwards.

The so-what line narrows eight rows to three. For life insurers, the first two rows, the bank counter and the rulebook, decide growth and margin. For health insurers, the fourth row, hospital inflation, decides profit.

A practical way to use the table: for each insurer you own, write down which row would hurt it most. A bank-led life insurer fears the first row. A savings-heavy one fears the second. A standalone health insurer fears the fourth. Then make sure your news alerts cover that row specifically.

c8.story:
If you want to understand why insurance stocks did what they did since 2023, read IRDAI's circulars, not the companies' results. Almost every reset in this industry started with a rule.

The regulator's big shift was from caps on commissions to a cap on total expenses as a share of premium, from April 2023. Insurers gained freedom to pay distributors what they liked, within an overall ceiling. In practice, the banks and large distributors used that freedom to ask for more, and the ceiling became the battleground.

Then came surrender values. From October 2024, a customer who stops paying early must get back much more of their money. That is plainly fairer to the customer. It also cut the margin insurers had earned on early quitters, and insurers responded by deferring commissions so that distributors share the pain when a policy lapses.

The GST change of September 2025 cut both ways. Individual life and health premiums were exempted, so a policy became cheaper overnight for the buyer. But an exempt product cannot claim input tax credit, so the GST insurers paid on commissions, rent and services became a pure cost. Volumes rose; margins took a hit.

In December 2025 Parliament allowed foreign insurers to own an Indian insurer outright. That opens the door to fresh capital, to foreign partners buying out their Indian joint-venture partners or exiting, and to more competition, especially in health.

Two more are on the horizon. Risk-based capital will tie solvency to the actual risks an insurer carries, rather than a flat formula. A new accounting standard will report profit over the life of the policy. And Bima Sugam, a regulator-backed online marketplace, could one day let customers buy and claim without a bank or broker in between, which would shift power away from the channel that holds it today.

In this industry, the regulator is not a background condition. It is the second management team.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who or what, what it does, why it matters, and the status.

  • Always: IRDAI itself, and the motor third-party price set with the road transport ministry. Note the IRDAI row's reason: every margin reset in this sector started with an IRDAI circular.
  • Live: expense limits, surrender value rules and the income tax regimes. These are shaping margins and demand today. The tax row matters more each year, as more taxpayers move to the new regime, which gives no deduction for premiums.
  • New: the GST exemption on retail life and health, and full foreign ownership. Both arrived in 2025, and their effects are still working through: one on volumes and margins, the other on ownership and competition.
  • Coming: risk-based capital with the new accounting standard, and Bima Sugam. These are the rules to prepare for, and they are why the rule on card eleven shows a cross for no new rule shock.

The quickest way to use this table is to read the coming rows as a list of possible future margin resets. Risk-based capital could free capital for well-diversified insurers and demand more from concentrated ones. The new accounting will change reported profit patterns without changing the cash. Bima Sugam would, if it works, lower distribution costs and weaken bank power, good for insurers with weak channels, less so for those whose moat is the bank counter.

Dated regulatory news for insurance, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab. IRDAI exposure drafts are the documents to read, because a draft today is a rule in a year.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces ask one question: once the money comes in, who gets to keep it? Insurance gives a surprising answer. The biggest threat is not a rival insurer. It is the seller.

Take life insurance first. The supplier is not a raw-material vendor; it is the bank or agent who supplies the customer. A large bank that sells most of an insurer's policies can and does bargain hard on commissions, and since the 2022 rule letting banks partner with more insurers, it has more leverage than ever. That is why the supplier spoke is the longest for life insurers.

The buyer, by contrast, is weak. A family buying a term policy or a savings plan rarely compares prices across insurers; it trusts the bank manager or the agent. That weakness is the life insurers' quiet advantage, and it is what lets a bank-backed life insurer keep a decent margin despite a powerful channel.

General and health insurance flips the buyer story. An employer renewing group health for thousands of staff runs a tender every year. A fleet owner shops motor rates. And the state general insurers have a history of pricing group health and fire to keep market share, which drags rates down for everyone. So rivalry and buyer power are both higher.

New entrants are a growing force, especially in health. Insurance licences need large capital, but full foreign ownership and fresh licences are bringing newcomers, and Go Digit showed in a few years that a digital-first general insurer can scale fast.

Substitutes split the doors cleanly. A savings plan competes with mutual funds, fixed deposits and gold, and in recent years it has often lost. Nothing substitutes for health or motor cover. You cannot buy a mutual fund to pay a hospital bill.

A savings plan has many rivals. A hospital bill has none.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches, the more pressure, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn, life insurers and general plus health insurers, and they cross. Neither is simply smaller.

  • The life shape reaches further on supplier, the bank and agent channel, and on substitutes, the funds, deposits and gold that compete with savings plans.
  • The general and health shape reaches further on rivalry, buyer and new entrants: many players, state insurers pricing for share, employers and fleet owners shopping every year, and new licences arriving.

Look at the shortest spoke on the chart: buyer power for life insurers, at the low end. That is the life insurers' moat drawn as a line: retail buyers rarely shop on price. The shortest spoke for general and health is substitutes, also near the low end: nothing replaces a health or motor cover.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with a reason. Use it to adjust for a specific company. A life insurer whose parent bank sells only its policies deserves a shorter supplier spoke; one dependent on an open-architecture bank deserves a longer one. A health insurer selling mostly retail through its own agents deserves a shorter buyer spoke than one heavy in group business. The so-what line puts the conclusion simply: life insurers with a captive bank keep the most, and general insurers keep profit only when they refuse to chase state-insurer pricing.

c10.story:
Insurance results are notoriously hard to read. Reported profit tells you little for a life insurer, premium growth can be bought with keener pricing, and the accounting is full of reserves and adjustments. Eight numbers cut through it, and they differ by door.

For life insurers, start with value of new business, the present value of future profits from this period's sales, and its margin, value of new business divided by sales. This is the single best measure of whether a life insurer is selling profitably. Then annualised premium equivalent, a way of counting new sales that treats a regular annual premium and a one-off single premium on a like-for-like basis. Then product mix: protection and non-linked plans earn the most, unit-linked plans the least. A rising share of protection is the best sign you can see in a life insurer's presentation.

Then persistency, the share of customers still paying after a year, and after five. This is the honesty test. A policy sold properly keeps being paid; a mis-sold one lapses. High persistency means the sales were genuine.

For general and health insurers, the key number is the combined ratio, claims plus costs as a share of premium. Below a hundred per cent means underwriting profit before any float income.

For all of them: the solvency ratio, the capital cushion above the regulator's floor, which tells you whether growth will require a share sale; premium growth against the market, which tells you about share gains; and return on embedded value or equity, which tells you whether growth earns more than capital costs.

For a life insurer, persistency is the polygraph. Customers who keep paying were sold the right policy.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • The first four rows are life-insurer numbers: value of new business and its margin, annualised premium equivalent, product mix and persistency. Read them as a chain: sales volume, then what kind of sales, then whether they stick, then what they are worth.
  • The fifth row, the combined ratio, is for general and health insurers. Note its two benchmarks: below a hundred overall, and lower still for retail health.
  • The last three rows apply to everyone: solvency, premium growth and return on embedded value or equity.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures. Persistency carries two marks, early and late; the gap between them shows how many customers drop off over the years.
  • Today's industry median shows a value only for premium growth, from the listed insurers' latest annual filings. Every other row shows a dash, because standard filing lines do not carry insurance metrics like value of new business or the combined ratio. Those come from each insurer's public disclosures and investor presentation.

Use the table as a checklist, door by door. For a life insurer, fill in the first four rows plus solvency and return on embedded value. For a general or health insurer, the combined ratio, solvency, premium growth and return on equity. Then read the premium growth median with care: it averages life and general insurers, so it shows the industry's direction rather than a benchmark for any one company.

c11.story:
Insurance is one of the few industries where much of the quarter's sales is published before the quarter ends. Life insurers' new-business premiums are released monthly through the industry council; general insurers' premiums are published monthly too. So the same-quarter dots on this chart are not guesses; they are the quarter's volume, almost line by line, weeks before results. Vehicle registrations, which bring new motor policies, and catastrophe claims from floods and cyclones also land in the same quarter.

One quarter ahead sit two signals. IRDAI circulars and consultation papers: a paper today is next year's margin, and a final rule hits the quarter it applies. And the Nifty's trailing return, because good markets lift unit-linked plan sales a quarter later.

Two quarters ahead are the slowest, most powerful signals. A Union Budget tax change creates a rush before it takes effect and a slump afterwards, as the 2023 budget did with high-ticket savings plans. And hospital tariff hikes show up in health claims within two quarters, before premiums can be repriced.

Put them together and the rule has three signs. Insurers are in an up-cycle when retail sales are growing in double digits, life margins and health combined ratios are stable or improving, and the regulator is not changing the economics. Today the first two hold: retail sales are strong after the GST removal, and margins, reset lower, are now holding. The third does not: risk-based capital and the new accounting standard are pending.

Two of three, which the rule calls early recovery. That is why the call prefers private life insurers with a protection-heavy mix and disciplined retail health insurers: they benefit most from the volume recovery and are least exposed if the next rule bites.
